## Required output shape

Every write-up you produce under this skill has these six labelled parts, in this order. The labels are literal — a reader greps for them. If a part has nothing in it, write the label and say so; an empty part named is worth more than a full one implied.

```
**Looked at:** <each source you actually consulted, with the count it returned>

## Observations
- <one fact per bullet, each with where it came from>

## What I make of it
- <your reading, each pointing back to an observation above>

**Not covered:** <what you could not reach, could not read, or may not say>

**Checked:** <what you re-verified against its source, and anything you corrected>
```

You may add sections of your own between these — tables, per-person breakdowns, whatever the material needs. You may not drop one of the six or rename it.

## How to fill them

**Looked at.** Say what you consulted and what came back, per source. Only what you really consulted. If you consulted nothing, write `Looked at: nothing — answering from what was already in front of me.` That is an accurate sentence and it is far better than a check you did not run.

**Observations.** Only what is the case. Every bullet carries its origin: a date, a conversation, a memory, a tool result, or "you said so in this conversation". Nothing here may contain *because*, *therefore*, *suggests* or *means* — those words belong in the next section. An interpretation that has drifted into the observations cannot be argued with, because it looks like a fact.

**What I make of it.** Your reading, and this is where *because* and *suggests* belong. Every claim points back to at least one observation above.

If something happened once, write "once" beside it. Do not call a single occurrence a tendency or a habit. To claim a pattern, count the instances and give the count. Two is a coincidence you noticed — say that.

Report outcomes, not requests. Not "I searched my history" but what came back and what it means for the question. And name what a failure would have looked like, so a reader can see the result was not guaranteed: "if he had never mentioned it, this would have returned nothing."

**Not covered.** What you could not reach, could not read, or chose not to say. If disclosure rules stopped you from repeating something, say that you cannot say it — never that it does not exist. Those are different facts and only one of them is yours to report.

**Checked.** Do this stage last and do it for real: re-read what you wrote and test each number, date and count against the source it came from. Then list what you checked. If you find an error, correct it in place and say so here — a correction on this line is the most valuable sentence in the document. If you checked nothing, write `Checked: nothing`, and know that it reads as exactly what it is.

Note which source you check against. A count from one tool is not verified by a different tool that counts something else; a conversation count and a message count are not the same number, and comparing them will invent an error that is not there.

## What this skill does not do

It does not tell you what to think, and it does not make a thin finding thicker. If the honest answer is short, the document is short — all six labels still appear and most are one line. A long document about very little is worse than a short one.

Nothing you write while following this becomes a memory of yours unless you decide it should and say so. The procedure is mine; the findings are yours.
